  --- D4 — Emergency Action Plan — Portland Facility
      file: 01-eap-chemical.pdf
      kind: program · status: gaps_found · shown as: needs_work

      what the reading said it is: This is the company's own written emergency action plan for the Portland facility. It covers the alarm system, evacuation and shelter-in-place, headcounts, first aid, and training. Oregon OSHA's emergency action plan rule (OAR 437-002-0042) governs it. The plan is written well but has holes: it does not say how to report an emergency, it does not name anyone to contact about the plan, and it does not say what happens to chemical processes when people evacuate. It was last revised in February 2021, even though it promises a review every January.
      WHAT THE READING FOUND WRONG WITH IT (6) — these are already findings; carry them, do not re-find them:
        · No procedure for reporting a fire or other emergency
            The plan says pull stations are at each exit door and that the alarm is monitored. It never tells employees how to report an emergency: pull the station, call 911, whom to tell inside the company, or how to report a chemical release or medical emergency. The only related line says emergency medical services 'are called', without saying who calls or how.
            what it needs: Add a short 'Reporting an emergency' section. Say who pulls the alarm, who calls 911 and from which phones, and who inside the company must be told (for example the incident coordinator or facilities lead). Say how to report a chemical spill or release that does not set off the alarm.
            the rule: OAR 437-002-0042(2) (minimum plan elements: procedures for reporting a fire or other emergency); the federal equivalent is 29 CFR 1910.38(c)(1). The exact paragraph letter in the Oregon rule was not checked.
        · No procedure for shutting down chemical processes before evacuating  [worked out from the document, not stated in it]
            This is a chemical manufacturing site. The plan tells everyone to leave and to 'secure nothing that requires more than a few seconds'. It does not say whether any process, reactor, heating or transfer operation must be shut down or made safe. It also does not say who does that, or that no one stays behind. The only shutdown step mentioned is turning off building ventilation during shelter-in-place.
            what it needs: State plainly either that no employee stays behind to run or shut down critical operations, or name the job titles that shut down specific equipment and when they must leave. Tie the section to the actual processes in the lab and warehouse.
            the rule: OAR 437-002-0042(2) (procedures for employees who remain to operate critical plant operations before they evacuate); the federal equivalent is 29 CFR 1910.38(c)(3). The exact paragraph letter in the Oregon rule was not checked.
        · No named contact for questions about the plan
            The rule requires the names or job titles of the people employees can contact for more information about the plan or their duties under it. The plan mentions a 'facilities lead' and an 'incident coordinator'. It never says who the incident coordinator is, and it does not name any contact for questions.
            what it needs: Add a contacts section. Give the name or job title (and phone number) of the plan owner and the incident coordinator, and of anyone employees can ask about their duties.
            the rule: OAR 437-002-0042(2)(f): 'Names or job titles of employees to contact for more information about the duties of employees under the plan.' The federal equivalent is 29 CFR 1910.38(c)(6).
        · Annual reviews not shown; plan not updated since 2021
            The plan promises a review every January, but it still carries the February 2021 revision date. There is no review log or sign-off. This is a gap against the plan's own commitment. It also matters under the rule, which says employees must be taken through the plan again whenever it changes.
            what it needs: Review the plan now. Update the headcount, the roster, the maps and the contacts. Add a revision and review log with dates and signatures, and keep records of the January reviews from now on.
            the rule: The plan's own Section 6. The rule's requirement to review the plan with employees when it changes is in OAR 437-002-0042 (federal equivalent: 29 CFR 1910.38(f)). The rule itself does not set a fixed review interval.
        · Earthquake is in scope but has no procedure
            Section 1 lists earthquakes among the emergencies the plan covers, but no section says what to do in one. The steps (drop, cover and hold on; do not evacuate while the shaking lasts; check for chemical spills afterwards) are different from fire evacuation. For a Portland chemical facility this is a real hazard.
            what it needs: Add a short earthquake section. Cover what to do during the shaking, when and how to evacuate afterwards, and how to check for chemical spills and damaged storage.
            the rule: None. This is an internal inconsistency, not a specific rule element.
        · Appendices not included in the file
            Appendix A (evacuation maps) and Appendix B (warden and first-aid roster) are listed but are not part of this file. So the exit route assignments and the named wardens and responders could not be checked.
            what it needs: Attach the current evacuation maps and the current roster to the file on record, with dates.
            the rule: OAR 437-002-0042(2) (evacuation procedures and exit route assignments); the federal equivalent is 29 CFR 1910.38(c)(2) and (e). The exact paragraph letter in the Oregon rule was not checked.
      DATES THIS DOCUMENT SETS (4):
        · Annual plan review by facilities lead (January reviews for 2022–2026 are not shown) — 2027-01-31 (recurring)
        · Annual training for floor wardens and first-aid responders — no date stated (recurring)
        · Autumn evacuation drill (twice-yearly drills, spring and autumn) — 2026-11-30 (recurring)
        · Monthly fire alarm test by facilities lead — 2026-10-05 (recurring)
      WHAT THE READING SAID A COMPANY LIKE THIS USUALLY ALSO HOLDS (7) —
        a suggestion from similar companies, NOT a checked requirement:
        · Chemical Hygiene Plan — The site has a laboratory, which often brings in the OSHA laboratory standard.
        · EPCRA Tier II hazardous chemical inventory report — Facilities storing hazardous chemicals above set amounts usually file every year with state and local emergency planners.
        · Evacuation drill records and alarm test logs — The plan commits to twice-yearly drills and monthly alarm tests; records would show they happen.
        · Fire Prevention Plan — Usually written alongside the emergency action plan for a facility storing flammable or reactive chemicals (OAR 437-002-0043).
        · Floor warden and first-aid/CPR/AED training records — The plan requires annual training for wardens and responders.
        · Hazard Communication Program and SDS inventory — The plan relies on SDSs being brought to responders; a chemical manufacturer would normally keep a written hazard communication program.
        · Spill response / SPCC or integrated contingency plan — Chemical manufacturers often hold spill or contingency plans for releases, and Oregon DEQ may regulate them.
      WHAT THIS DOCUMENT SAYS, proposed by the reading, not confirmed by anyone (6):

            it says: "trained first-aid responders (two per shift, named on the warden roster), who bring the first-aid kit and the AED from the front office"
            where: Section 5, page 4
        · chemical release hazard: Chemical releases are a recognized emergency at the site; the plan relies on evacuation, not employee response, as of 2021-02-01

            where: Sections 1, 3 and 5, pages 2–4
        · emergency eyewash shower: Emergency shower and eyewash at the loading dock, as of 2021-02-01
            it says: "taken to the emergency shower and eyewash at the loading dock"
            where: Section 5, page 4
        · employee count site: 42 employees at the Portland facility, as of 2021-02-01
            it says: "It applies to all 42 employees at the Portland facility"
            where: Section 1, page 2
        · fire alarm monitoring: Monitored fire alarm with horns and strobes, 24-hour monitoring by Cascade Fire & Safety under a service contract, as of 2021-02-01
            it says: "The alarm is monitored 24 hours a day by Cascade Fire & Safety under a service contract."
            where: Section 2, page 2

            it says: "including warehouse, drivers, laboratory and office staff"

  --- D5 — Employee Handbook Addendum: Food Safety Credentials and Paid Sick & Safe Time — Harbor Kitchen Ballard
      file: Harbor-Kitchen-Employee-Policy-2026.pdf
      kind: policy · status: gaps_found · shown as: needs_work
      the document's own date: 2026-11-01 (effective)
      the date that matters: 2026-11-01 (effective)
      what the reading said it is: This is an employee handbook addendum that establishes food safety credential requirements, alcohol service training rules, and paid sick and safe time (PSST) accrual and use policies for Harbor Kitchen's Ballard location (approximately 25 employees). The addendum addresses federal, state, and city labor law obligations for restaurants in Seattle.
      WHAT THE READING FOUND WRONG WITH IT (9) — these are already findings; carry them, do not re-find them:
        · Food Worker Card Timeline Mismatch
            The policy states new kitchen hires have 30 days to obtain a card, but Washington State law requires the card within 14 days of hire. This gives kitchen staff 16 extra days of non-compliance.
            what it needs: Revise Section 1 to state that all kitchen staff must obtain a valid Washington State Food Worker Card within 14 days of starting employment, not 30 days.
            the rule: Washington State Administrative Code Chapter 246-217 (RCW 69.07.015)
        · PSST Eligibility Excludes Covered Employees
            The policy states that part-time and seasonal staff are not eligible for PSST. However, Seattle's PSST Ordinance (SMC 14.16) explicitly covers all employees working in Seattle regardless of employment status (full-time, part-time, temporary, or seasonal). The policy violates this requirement.
            what it needs: Revise the Eligibility row in the PSST table to state: 'All employees (full-time, part-time, seasonal, and temporary) who work in Seattle are covered and accrue PSST. Only the waiting period and carryover caps vary by tier.'
            the rule: Seattle Municipal Code Section 14.16.025 and Seattle Office of Labor Standards guidance
        · PSST Carryover Cap Exceeds Legal Maximum
            The policy states up to 24 hours of unused PSST carries over to the following year. However, for Tier 1 employers (1-49 FTEs), Seattle law requires a minimum carryover cap of 40 hours, not a maximum of 24 hours. Harbor Kitchen Ballard qualifies as Tier 1 with approximately 25 employees. The policy provides less leave than required.
            what it needs: Revise the Annual carryover row to state: 'Up to 40 hours of unused PSST carries over to the following year.' This is the minimum required for Tier 1 employers.
            the rule: Seattle Municipal Code Section 14.16.025 and Section 14.16.030; Seattle Labor Standards Ordinance
        · PSST Waiting Period Exceeds Legal Maximum
            The policy states employees may begin using PSST after 180 days of employment. However, Seattle law allows employers to impose a maximum waiting period of 90 days. The 180-day period is nearly double the legal limit and denies employees their right to use accrued leave.
            what it needs: Revise the Waiting period row to state: 'Employees may begin using PSST after no more than 90 days of employment.' Accrued hours remain available for use starting on the 90th day.
            the rule: Seattle Municipal Code Section 14.16.035 and Seattle Office of Labor Standards guidance
        · Shift Coverage Penalty Not Permitted
            The policy states that if an employee cannot find a co-worker to cover a shift requested for PSST use, the absence may be recorded as unexcused. This penalizes employees for exercising their legal right to PSST. Seattle law does not permit employers to condition use of accrued PSST on employee-secured shift coverage or to mark such absences as unexcused.
            what it needs: Remove the shift coverage requirement language entirely. Revise to: 'PSST is a guaranteed benefit and does not require finding coverage. Employees may use accrued PSST upon request.'
            the rule: Seattle Municipal Code Section 14.16.025 and .035; Seattle Office of Labor Standards interpretive guidance
        · Tips-Toward-Minimum Violation for Tipped Employees
            The policy states: 'Tips received are credited toward this minimum for tipped positions.' This is illegal under Washington State law. Washington does not permit tip credits; the minimum wage of $20.76/hour must be paid in cash regardless of tips received. Tips are the employee's property and cannot be counted toward the minimum wage obligation.
            what it needs: Remove all language crediting tips toward minimum wage. Revise to: 'Ballard staff are paid the Seattle minimum wage of $20.76 per hour. Tips received are the employee's to retain and are not credited toward this minimum.'
            the rule: Washington State Minimum Wage Act (RCW 49.46.020); Washington State Department of Labor & Industries
        · Missing MAST Training Deadline Specification  [worked out from the document, not stated in it]
            The policy states bartenders must complete MAST training within 60 days of hire but does not specify the consequences of non-completion or how the restaurant will verify and document completion. Washington State requires proof of training for bartenders and servers who serve alcohol. The policy should make clear what evidence is required.
            what it needs: Add language specifying: 'Proof of completion (certificate or training card) must be retained by the restaurant for verification by state or local alcohol control agents. Employees who fail to complete MAST training within 60 days may not serve alcohol.'
            the rule: Washington State RCW 66.24.200 (On-Premise License) and Department of Liquor and Cannabis Board rules
        · Missing Written PSST Policy Requirements  [worked out from the document, not stated in it]
            Seattle law requires a comprehensive written PSST policy that covers paid leave rights, tier classification, accrual and carryover rules, notification procedures, allowed uses, and verification requirements. This addendum does not address the full scope required. Specifically missing: detailed allowed uses (sick time, safe time for DV/SA/stalking), verification procedures that don't impose unreasonable expenses on employees, and employee rights regarding confidentiality and non-retaliation.
            what it needs: Expand the PSST section to include: (1) explicit allowed uses (illness, preventive care, family care, safe time for domestic violence/sexual assault/stalking); (2) verification procedures that do not impose unreasonable cost on employees; (3) non-retaliation and confidentiality protections; (4) method and frequency of wage statement disclosures of accrued and used PSST.
            the rule: Seattle Municipal Code Section 14.16.025 and Section 14.16.035; Seattle Office of Labor Standards requirements
        · Inaccurate Tier Classification Statement
            The document states Harbor Kitchen Ballard 'is a Tier 1 employer under Seattle's Paid Sick and Safe Time Ordinance because this location has fewer than 50 employees.' However, tier classification depends on full-time equivalents (FTEs) worldwide across all locations, not just headcount at one location. Harbor Kitchen LLC owns two restaurants (Ballard with ~25 employees, Fremont with 31 employees), totaling ~56 employees. This may push the company into Tier 2 (50–249 FTEs), which has different accrual and carryover requirements. The tier must be verified based on worldwide FTE count.
            what it needs: Revise the tier classification statement to: 'Tier classification is based on the worldwide full-time equivalent count of Harbor Kitchen LLC across all locations. Please confirm current tier status with the Seattle Office of Labor Standards, as requirements may differ by tier.'
            the rule: Seattle Municipal Code Section 14.16.005; Seattle Labor Standards Interpretive Guidance
      WHAT THIS DOCUMENT OBLIGES THEM TO KEEP DOING (5), read out of the document itself:
        · WAC 246-217 — Food Worker Card Maintenance
            the evidence you would expect to see: Valid Washington State Food Worker Card for each kitchen staff member, maintained by the employee and verifiable by health department during inspection
        · RCW 66.24.200 — MAST Training Verification
            the evidence you would expect to see: Certificate or training card showing completion of MAST training within 60 days of hire, retained by the restaurant for inspection
        · SMC 14.16.025 and 14.16.030 — PSST Accrual and Carryover (if Tier 1 confirmed)
            the evidence you would expect to see: Payroll records and wage statements showing proper accrual at 1 hour per 40 worked, carryover of unused hours (minimum 40 hours for Tier 1), and no penalty on use
        · RCW 49.46.020 and SMC 14.20.020 — Seattle Minimum Wage Payment
            the evidence you would expect to see: Payroll records showing all employees paid at least $20.76/hour in direct wages; tips documented separately and retained by employees
        · Washington labor law and Seattle ordinance requirements — Workplace Posters Display
            the evidence you would expect to see: Posters displayed at the Ballard location (and all locations) covering minimum wage, PSST, overtime, and workplace rights
      DATES THIS DOCUMENT SETS (3):
        · Food Worker Card Completion for New Kitchen Hires — no date stated
        · MAST Training Completion for Bartenders — no date stated
        · Policy Implementation and Correction — 2026-11-03
      WHAT THE READING SAID A COMPANY LIKE THIS USUALLY ALSO HOLDS (4) —
        a suggestion from similar companies, NOT a checked requirement:
        · Certified Food Protection Manager Verification — Washington State Retail Food Code requires food service establishments to have a certified food protection manager on staff or available.
        · Employee Rights Notice and Postings — Seattle requires specific postings on minimum wage, PSST, wage theft ordinance, and other labor standards to be displayed prominently; this addendum only mentions posters 'available on request.'
        · Payroll Records and Wage Statement Requirements — Washington State law requires itemized wage statements showing gross pay, deductions, hours worked, accrual and use of PSST for each pay period.
        · Sexual Harassment and Discrimination Prevention Policy — Washington State and federal law require employers to have written policies on workplace harassment, discrimination, and retaliation prevention.

Emergency Action Plan — Portland Facility
documents.summary: This is the company's own written emergency action plan for the Portland facility. It covers the alarm system, evacuation and shelter-in-place, headcounts, first aid, and training. Oregon OSHA's emergency action plan rule (OAR 437-002-0042) governs it. The plan is written well but has holes: it does not say how to report an emergency, it does not name anyone to contact about the plan, and it does not say what happens to chemical processes when people evacuate. It was last revised in February 2021, even though it promises a review every January.

open_gaps.title: No procedure for reporting a fire or other emergency
open_gaps.description: The plan says pull stations are at each exit door and that the alarm is monitored. It never tells employees how to report an emergency: pull the station, call 911, whom to tell inside the company, or how to report a chemical release or medical emergency. The only related line says emergency medical services 'are called', without saying who calls or how.
open_gaps.fix: Add a short 'Reporting an emergency' section. Say who pulls the alarm, who calls 911 and from which phones, and who inside the company must be told (for example the incident coordinator or facilities lead). Say how to report a chemical spill or release that does not set off the alarm.
open_gaps.citation: OAR 437-002-0042(2) (minimum plan elements: procedures for reporting a fire or other emergency); the federal equivalent is 29 CFR 1910.38(c)(1). The exact paragraph letter in the Oregon rule was not checked.

open_gaps.title: No procedure for shutting down chemical processes before evacuating
open_gaps.description: This is a chemical manufacturing site. The plan tells everyone to leave and to 'secure nothing that requires more than a few seconds'. It does not say whether any process, reactor, heating or transfer operation must be shut down or made safe. It also does not say who does that, or that no one stays behind. The only shutdown step mentioned is turning off building ventilation during shelter-in-place.
open_gaps.fix: State plainly either that no employee stays behind to run or shut down critical operations, or name the job titles that shut down specific equipment and when they must leave. Tie the section to the actual processes in the lab and warehouse.
open_gaps.citation: OAR 437-002-0042(2) (procedures for employees who remain to operate critical plant operations before they evacuate); the federal equivalent is 29 CFR 1910.38(c)(3). The exact paragraph letter in the Oregon rule was not checked.

open_gaps.title: No named contact for questions about the plan
open_gaps.description: The rule requires the names or job titles of the people employees can contact for more information about the plan or their duties under it. The plan mentions a 'facilities lead' and an 'incident coordinator'. It never says who the incident coordinator is, and it does not name any contact for questions.
open_gaps.fix: Add a contacts section. Give the name or job title (and phone number) of the plan owner and the incident coordinator, and of anyone employees can ask about their duties.
open_gaps.citation: OAR 437-002-0042(2)(f): 'Names or job titles of employees to contact for more information about the duties of employees under the plan.' The federal equivalent is 29 CFR 1910.38(c)(6).

open_gaps.title: Annual reviews not shown; plan not updated since 2021
open_gaps.description: The plan promises a review every January, but it still carries the February 2021 revision date. There is no review log or sign-off. This is a gap against the plan's own commitment. It also matters under the rule, which says employees must be taken through the plan again whenever it changes.
open_gaps.fix: Review the plan now. Update the headcount, the roster, the maps and the contacts. Add a revision and review log with dates and signatures, and keep records of the January reviews from now on.

documents.title: Employee Handbook Addendum: Food Safety Credentials and Paid Sick & Safe Time — Harbor Kitchen Ballard
documents.summary: This is an employee handbook addendum that establishes food safety credential requirements, alcohol service training rules, and paid sick and safe time (PSST) accrual and use policies for Harbor Kitchen's Ballard location (approximately 25 employees). The addendum addresses federal, state, and city labor law obligations for restaurants in Seattle.

open_gaps.title: Food Worker Card Timeline Mismatch
open_gaps.description: The policy states new kitchen hires have 30 days to obtain a card, but Washington State law requires the card within 14 days of hire. This gives kitchen staff 16 extra days of non-compliance.
open_gaps.fix: Revise Section 1 to state that all kitchen staff must obtain a valid Washington State Food Worker Card within 14 days of starting employment, not 30 days.
open_gaps.citation: Washington State Administrative Code Chapter 246-217 (RCW 69.07.015)

open_gaps.title: PSST Eligibility Excludes Covered Employees
open_gaps.description: The policy states that part-time and seasonal staff are not eligible for PSST. However, Seattle's PSST Ordinance (SMC 14.16) explicitly covers all employees working in Seattle regardless of employment status (full-time, part-time, temporary, or seasonal). The policy violates this requirement.
open_gaps.fix: Revise the Eligibility row in the PSST table to state: 'All employees (full-time, part-time, seasonal, and temporary) who work in Seattle are covered and accrue PSST. Only the waiting period and carryover caps vary by tier.'
open_gaps.citation: Seattle Municipal Code Section 14.16.025 and Seattle Office of Labor Standards guidance

open_gaps.title: PSST Carryover Cap Exceeds Legal Maximum
open_gaps.description: The policy states up to 24 hours of unused PSST carries over to the following year. However, for Tier 1 employers (1-49 FTEs), Seattle law requires a minimum carryover cap of 40 hours, not a maximum of 24 hours. Harbor Kitchen Ballard qualifies as Tier 1 with approximately 25 employees. The policy provides less leave than required.
open_gaps.fix: Revise the Annual carryover row to state: 'Up to 40 hours of unused PSST carries over to the following year.' This is the minimum required for Tier 1 employers.
open_gaps.citation: Seattle Municipal Code Section 14.16.025 and Section 14.16.030; Seattle Labor Standards Ordinance

open_gaps.title: PSST Waiting Period Exceeds Legal Maximum
open_gaps.description: The policy states employees may begin using PSST after 180 days of employment. However, Seattle law allows employers to impose a maximum waiting period of 90 days. The 180-day period is nearly double the legal limit and denies employees their right to use accrued leave.
open_gaps.fix: Revise the Waiting period row to state: 'Employees may begin using PSST after no more than 90 days of employment.' Accrued hours remain available for use starting on the 90th day.
open_gaps.citation: Seattle Municipal Code Section 14.16.035 and Seattle Office of Labor Standards guidance

open_gaps.title: Shift Coverage Penalty Not Permitted
open_gaps.description: The policy states that if an employee cannot find a co-worker to cover a shift requested for PSST use, the absence may be recorded as unexcused. This penalizes employees for exercising their legal right to PSST. Seattle law does not permit employers to condition use of accrued PSST on employee-secured shift coverage or to mark such absences as unexcused.
open_gaps.fix: Remove the shift coverage requirement language entirely. Revise to: 'PSST is a guaranteed benefit and does not require finding coverage. Employees may use accrued PSST upon request.'
open_gaps.citation: Seattle Municipal Code Section 14.16.025 and .035; Seattle Office of Labor Standards interpretive guidance

open_gaps.title: Tips-Toward-Minimum Violation for Tipped Employees
open_gaps.description: The policy states: 'Tips received are credited toward this minimum for tipped positions.' This is illegal under Washington State law. Washington does not permit tip credits; the minimum wage of $20.76/hour must be paid in cash regardless of tips received. Tips are the employee's property and cannot be counted toward the minimum wage obligation.
open_gaps.fix: Remove all language crediting tips toward minimum wage. Revise to: 'Ballard staff are paid the Seattle minimum wage of $20.76 per hour. Tips received are the employee's to retain and are not credited toward this minimum.'
open_gaps.citation: Washington State Minimum Wage Act (RCW 49.46.020); Washington State Department of Labor & Industries

open_gaps.title: Missing MAST Training Deadline Specification
open_gaps.description: The policy states bartenders must complete MAST training within 60 days of hire but does not specify the consequences of non-completion or how the restaurant will verify and document completion. Washington State requires proof of training for bartenders and servers who serve alcohol. The policy should make clear what evidence is required.
open_gaps.fix: Add language specifying: 'Proof of completion (certificate or training card) must be retained by the restaurant for verification by state or local alcohol control agents. Employees who fail to complete MAST training within 60 days may not serve alcohol.'
open_gaps.citation: Washington State RCW 66.24.200 (On-Premise License) and Department of Liquor and Cannabis Board rules

open_gaps.title: Missing Written PSST Policy Requirements
open_gaps.description: Seattle law requires a comprehensive written PSST policy that covers paid leave rights, tier classification, accrual and carryover rules, notification procedures, allowed uses, and verification requirements. This addendum does not address the full scope required. Specifically missing: detailed allowed uses (sick time, safe time for DV/SA/stalking), verification procedures that don't impose unreasonable expenses on employees, and employee rights regarding confidentiality and non-retaliation.
open_gaps.fix: Expand the PSST section to include: (1) explicit allowed uses (illness, preventive care, family care, safe time for domestic violence/sexual assault/stalking); (2) verification procedures that do not impose unreasonable cost on employees; (3) non-retaliation and confidentiality protections; (4) method and frequency of wage statement disclosures of accrued and used PSST.
open_gaps.citation: Seattle Municipal Code Section 14.16.025 and Section 14.16.035; Seattle Office of Labor Standards requirements

open_gaps.title: Inaccurate Tier Classification Statement
open_gaps.description: The document states Harbor Kitchen Ballard 'is a Tier 1 employer under Seattle's Paid Sick and Safe Time Ordinance because this location has fewer than 50 employees.' However, tier classification depends on full-time equivalents (FTEs) worldwide across all locations, not just headcount at one location. Harbor Kitchen LLC owns two restaurants (Ballard with ~25 employees, Fremont with 31 employees), totaling ~56 employees. This may push the company into Tier 2 (50–249 FTEs), which has different accrual and carryover requirements. The tier must be verified based on worldwide FTE count.
open_gaps.fix: Revise the tier classification statement to: 'Tier classification is based on the worldwide full-time equivalent count of Harbor Kitchen LLC across all locations. Please confirm current tier status with the Seattle Office of Labor Standards, as requirements may differ by tier.'
open_gaps.citation: Seattle Municipal Code Section 14.16.005; Seattle Labor Standards Interpretive Guidance

documents.summary: This is an internal spill response procedure for sodium hydroxide solution spills at Cascade Specialty Chemicals' Portland facility. open_gaps.title: Sodium hydroxide reportable quantity not aligned with Oregon DEQ rule
open_gaps.description: The procedure states 'Report any spill over 5 gallons' but Oregon DEQ requires reporting when spills meet or exceed the reportable quantity in 40 CFR 302.4. The CERCLA reportable quantity for sodium hydroxide is 1,000 pounds (approximately 500 gallons at 50% solution). Spills between 5 and 500 gallons would not trigger DEQ reporting under state law, contradicting the procedure's 5-gallon threshold.
open_gaps.fix: Revise the reporting threshold to align with Oregon DEQ requirements: report spills that meet or exceed the federal reportable quantity for sodium hydroxide under 40 CFR 302.4, which is 1,000 pounds. At 50% concentration (as stated in your SDS), this equals approximately 500 gallons of solution. Alternatively, clarify whether the 5-gallon threshold reflects a company-specific policy trigger that is stricter than regulatory minimums.

open_gaps.title: Reporting channel uses direct phone number instead of required emergency response system
open_gaps.description: The procedure instructs to 'Report any spill over 5 gallons to Oregon DEQ within 24 hours on 503-229-5696.' Oregon DEQ requires spills to be reported immediately (not within 24 hours) to the Oregon Emergency Response System at 1-800-452-0311. A direct DEQ phone line is not the designated emergency reporting mechanism.
open_gaps.fix: Revise to: 'Report any spill that meets or exceeds the reportable quantity immediately to the Oregon Emergency Response System at 1-800-452-0311.' Reserve the DEQ regional office phone number for follow-up spill release reports after cleanup is underway or complete.

open_gaps.description: The procedure assigns spill response duties to employees (evacuate, don PPE, contain, neutralize) but does not state that employees must receive hazardous waste operations and emergency response training before performing these tasks. OSHA 29 CFR 1910.120 requires proper training and equipment for employees who may respond to hazmat spills.
open_gaps.fix: Add a section stating: 'Only employees who have completed OSHA Hazardous Waste Operations and Emergency Response (HAZWOPER) training, as required under 29 CFR 1910.120, are authorized to respond to spills. Persons assigned to perform spill response must hold a current training certificate on file with the EHS lead.'
open_gaps.citation: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.120 (Hazardous Waste Operations and Emergency Response Standard)

open_gaps.title: No guidance on preventing water contact during neutralization with citric acid
open_gaps.description: The procedure directs operators to 'Neutralise with citric acid from the spill kit until pH is between 6 and 9.' Sodium hydroxide solution can generate significant heat when contacted by water or acidic material. The SDS for sodium hydroxide notes that contact with water or moisture may generate enough heat to ignite combustibles. The procedure does not warn about thermal hazard during neutralization or specify the method for safe acid addition.
open_gaps.fix: Revise step 4 to: 'Carefully add citric acid from the spill kit in small increments while monitoring temperature. Avoid rapid mixing. Continue until pH indicator shows pH 6–9. Do not allow water to contact the sodium hydroxide solution directly, as the reaction may generate heat sufficient to ignite combustibles.'

open_gaps.title: No mention of preventing drainage to drains, sewers, or waterways
open_gaps.description: The procedure does not instruct responders to prevent spilled material from entering drains, sewers, or waterways. Sodium hydroxide solutions must be kept out of these systems to prevent environmental damage. Standard OSHA and industry guidance for sodium hydroxide spills includes this critical containment step.
open_gaps.fix: Add after step 3 (Contain the spill): 'Ensure spill material cannot flow into floor drains, storm drains, or sewer systems. Dike or block drainage pathways as necessary. Do not flush spill residue down any drain.'
open_gaps.citation: OSHA best practices and Sodium Hydroxide SDS emergency procedures; OAR 340-142 environmental protection requirements

open_gaps.title: No documented location or availability of spill kit materials
open_gaps.description: The procedure references 'the spill kit' and 'absorbent socks stored on rack B' but does not verify that these materials are actually stocked, inspected, or maintained. open_gaps.fix: Create and maintain a spill kit inventory log showing: (1) location (e.g., rack B); (2) contents (type and quantity of absorbent pads, socks, citric acid, etc.); (3) date last verified; (4) expiration date of any perishable items; (5) date of next inspection. open_gaps.citation: OSHA 1910.1450 (Occupational Exposure to Hazardous Chemicals in Laboratories) and general emergency preparedness best practices

open_gaps.title: No instruction to prevent personnel exposure during evacuation and response
open_gaps.description: While the procedure tells responders to 'Put on a face shield, chemical gloves and a rubber apron,' it does not address respiratory protection or skin protection for the person evacuating others or containing the spill. OSHA and SDS guidance for sodium hydroxide solutions recommend respiratory protection if dust or mist is present. The procedure should specify whether the west bay has adequate ventilation and whether respirators must be available.

documents.title: Spill Response Procedure — Caustic Soda
documents.summary: This is a procedural document outlining Cascade's process for responding to spills of sodium hydroxide (caustic soda) at the Portland facility. It provides step-by-step instructions for containment, neutralization, and cleanup, along with a threshold-based reporting obligation to Oregon DEQ for spills exceeding 5 gallons within 24 hours. The document is part of the facility's emergency preparedness program and must be reviewed and updated annually.

open_gaps.title: Missing PPE and eyewash/shower requirements
open_gaps.description: The procedure instructs staff to put on PPE from a cabinet but does not reference whether eyewash and shower stations are located and accessible. OSHA 29 CFR 1910.151 requires emergency eyewash and shower facilities for facilities using corrosive chemicals like sodium hydroxide.
open_gaps.fix: Add a statement confirming the location and accessibility of emergency eyewash and shower stations, or specify how staff will access them if a larger exposure occurs.
open_gaps.citation: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.151

open_gaps.title: Missing post-spill medical evaluation or exposure monitoring language
open_gaps.description: The procedure does not state whether workers involved in spill response should receive medical evaluation or whether inhalation/skin contact exposure should be monitored or reported.
open_gaps.fix: Add language requiring medical evaluation for any worker with inhalation or skin contact exposure, and specify documentation and reporting to the EHS lead.
open_gaps.citation: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1200 (Hazard Communication); OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1000 Table Z-1 (Sodium Hydroxide PEL 2 mg/m³)

open_gaps.title: Unclear spill reporting threshold vs. CERCLA RQ
open_gaps.description: The procedure requires reporting to Oregon DEQ for spills over 5 gallons within 24 hours. However, the CERCLA reportable quantity for sodium hydroxide is 1,000 pounds (approximately 300 gallons of a 50% solution). Oregon may have its own threshold, but the document does not clarify whether this 5-gallon local reporting obligation applies alongside or instead of federal CERCLA reporting, or whether the threshold aligns with state hazardous-waste rules.
open_gaps.fix: Clarify whether the 5-gallon threshold is the state environmental reporting requirement under Oregon Administrative Rule or another rule. If it differs from federal CERCLA (1,000 lb RQ), confirm which rule(s) apply and add a note that CERCLA reporting may apply separately for larger spills.
open_gaps.citation: Oregon Administrative Rule 340-142-0040 (Spill Reporting); 40 CFR 302.4 (CERCLA Reportable Quantities)

open_gaps.title: Missing neutralization verification language
open_gaps.description: The procedure states to neutralize with citric acid until pH is between 6 and 9, but does not specify how pH will be verified (e.g., pH test strips, meter) or who will perform the check.
open_gaps.fix: Specify the method for verifying pH (e.g., pH paper or portable pH meter) and confirm that the person performing neutralization is trained to use it. Document the initial and final pH values.
open_gaps.citation: Best practice under OSHA Hazard Communication; referenced in SDS spill response sections

open_gaps.title: Missing prevention and training requirements
open_gaps.description: The procedure does not address worker training on spill response, equipment inspection, or preventive measures to avoid spills (e.g., pump maintenance, transfer procedures, overfill prevention).
open_gaps.fix: Add sections on initial and annual training requirements for all employees who may encounter or respond to sodium hydroxide spills, and specify maintenance and inspection schedules for pumps and transfer equipment.
open_gaps.citation: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1200 (Hazard Communication training); OSHA 1910.119 or similar if Process Safety Management applies; Oregon OSHA rules.

open_gaps.title: Missing documentation and investigation language

open_gaps.fix: Add a requirement for a post-incident report including: date, time, quantity spilled, cause, response actions, cleanup time, any exposures or injuries, and lessons learned. Specify who completes the report and where it is filed.
